A clear demonstration is made. For if the discussion were about bodies, either our own or others, and it were to attribute the properties of bodies to them, even if it seemed to happen naturally to things that are generated and corrupted, it would not be unseemly. However, it is acknowledged that the path to existence is not about what does not exist at all. But it will also endure the divisions from the one who begets to the individualization of the one who is begotten. And concerning the highest of all substances, the one beyond all generated things, how can it not be absurd to accept divisions and separations, and to seek generation in time? Away with foolishness, human! For you are introducing a weak notion to the things being contemplated, and you are not entering into the truth. Or do you know the divine nature, attributing the properties of bodies to it, and diminishing its superiority, which is above and beyond all created things, to a more shameful glory? For the Father is always the Father, and not from the power that proceeds in time to beget, but it is necessary that the one through whom he is Father always coexists. For 'in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God,' according to the Scriptures. And where the 'was' is named, with nothing preceding it, where will the course of thought stop, and to what end will it arrive, as if the mind were to pursue the 'was' in weak imaginations? Therefore, the Word was begotten, and the Word was God; and it was begotten, not according to the nature of the body, as if to think of otherness in existence for the begotten towards the one who begets.

We necessarily use the name of birth from what is ours, signifying that the Only-Begotten of the Father's substance shone forth as light by law; and he subsists individually and is conceived in his own existence; the discourse about this is entirely ineffable; for he does not exist by virtue of the begetter's substance, but rather, being himself and existing in the Father, he shows the begetter in his own nature and is worshiped and glorified together; since he is of the same substance and equal in glory, he is necessarily co-working and equal in strength; with the Holy Spirit subsisting together with us and being theologized and perceived together, the faith about the Holy Trinity is rightly and blamelessly conceived; the one who is well-suited to the dignities of God and the Father, through whom all things were brought forth to birth, did not consider being equal to God a thing to be grasped, but rather emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming like men; and being found in the appearance of a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross; although he was able to revel in his own superiority and equality with the Father and to luxuriate in the riches of divinity, he willingly descended to our form, not being wronged in his own nature by the assumption of the inferior, but rather adding what was needed to himself

For it was not likely, rather it was most dangerous to think and say that human nature might somehow surpass and forcibly drag the divine and ineffable nature to its own level, and according to its own superiority. But it is wise, as I think, to reason that we must yield to the nature of divinity. And indeed, it will be much better to be overcome by the glory of what is prior. For it is one of the most absurd things to see in the things done by God a mixture and addition of better things, and the not very beautiful things being adorned. To think that God has spoken with human nature in the way that He Himself knows, and not rather to have somehow imparted some of His own, and to have lifted up the unworthy nature to His own. And the sun, by the touch of its rays, and by pouring into the mire and marshes, will completely preserve its light unharmed. But the divine and uncorrupted, and supreme nature, either can suffer something of the things that are accustomed to grieve, or how can it be wronged in its association with the lesser? How can it not surpass the nature of the worse, and by its own goods illuminate and transfer it to the much better? Therefore, those who are ungrateful for the things that should be admired, and who are puffed up with pride, are sick with the disease of haughtiness. And they think that they share in the divine glory, defining the unseemly as part of the best economy. For they do not accept the mystery.

But laughing, they think the matter is foolish, and they say we are compared to lifeless objects. Not understanding that their own teachers, if they had grasped something to think or say, would have difficulty in keeping the faith and the saying 'He himself said', and then they would have opposed their own thoughts to the divine judgments, pouring them into their own heads with great difficulty. Nor do they honor these things with the divine nature. But someone, as they think, has thoroughly investigated the matter. For how, they say, can the undefiled mind, which is free from quantity and definition, be enclosed in a human body? I, however, praise the fact that the divine transcends the quantity of bodies. I will agree, for I say that nevertheless those who think in this way have made a choice. We do not say that the nature of the Word can be defined, even if it is said to dwell in the holy body of the Virgin, but rather that it fills the heavens as God, and the earth, and the things below, and is not absent from any of the whole. And there was also a human being after this. But as for how or in what way, if you are unable to understand, yield to the things beyond the mind, and grant silence to the things beyond reason. There are many other things that they do not know. For where has the earth been established? What foundation does the heaven have? And in what way has the chorus of the stars been made, and the path that is above and on high? But if someone were to choose to speak about each of these things, I think they would spend a long time on words, composing narratives for you.

But they say that it is a small thing for God who is above all to become like us; you accuse because being philanthropic and good by nature, He has taken more care for us than is fitting; for it is acknowledged that it is a small thing for Him to become like us, which is called kenosis; but the word of His gentleness towards us will be shown to be consistent with Scripture; what is truly worthy of wonder is that He has taken on the causes of our salvation, and one might ask how He has done this without being impious; tell me, then, whether you think it would have been better for Him to leave us bound by our sins, or rather to save us and show us care; how can one doubt that it is fitting for the good God to distribute goods to those who have come from Him; how can some people still claim that Scripture and the economy of salvation are without blame; we will allow doctors to deal with the treatment of passions, but we will rebuke God for not being ignorant of the way of our care
pass_b_english: The discussion at hand presents a clear demonstration, one that is evident and unmistakable. If the topic were about physical bodies, whether our own or others, and it were to attribute the characteristics of bodies to them, it would not be unreasonable, even if it seemed to occur naturally in the context of generated and corrupted things.

However, it is acknowledged that the path to existence is not about what does not exist at all. Instead, it will also endure the divisions that arise from the one who begets to the individualization of the one who is begotten. Furthermore, when considering the highest of all substances, the one that transcends all generated things, it is absurd to accept divisions and separations, and to seek generation in time.

The notion that the divine nature can be attributed with the properties of bodies is misguided, and it diminishes the superiority of God, which is above and beyond all created things, to a more shameful glory. The Father is always the Father, and not from the power that proceeds in time to beget, but it is necessary that the one through whom he is Father always coexists. As the Scriptures state, 'in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God' (Genesis 1:1). The concept of the 'was' is complex, and it challenges the course of thought, leading to a pursuit of understanding that is difficult to grasp.

We necessarily use the name of birth from what is ours, signifying that the Only-Begotten of the Father's substance shone forth as light by law. He subsists individually and is conceived in his own existence, and the discourse about this is entirely ineffable. For he does not exist by virtue of the begetter's substance, but rather, being himself and existing in the Father, he shows the begetter in his own nature and is worshiped and glorified together. Since he is of the same substance and equal in glory, he is necessarily co-working and equal in strength.

With the Holy Spirit subsisting together with us and being theologized and perceived together, the faith about the Holy Trinity is rightly and blamelessly conceived. The one who is well-suited to the dignities of God and the Father, through whom all things were brought forth to birth, did not consider being equal to God a thing to be grasped, but rather emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming like men (Philippians 2:7); and being found in the appearance of a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8). Although he was able to revel in his own superiority and equality with the Father and to luxuriate in the riches of divinity, he willingly descended to our form, not being wronged in his own nature by the assumption of the inferior, but rather adding what was needed to himself.

It is not likely that human nature could surpass the divine and ineffable nature, and forcibly drag it to its own level. Rather, it is most dangerous to even think or say such a thing. The idea that human nature could overcome the divine nature and bring it down to its own level is not only absurd, but also harmful. On the other hand, it is wise to reason that we must yield to the nature of divinity, and allow it to surpass us. We do not say that the nature of the Word can be defined, for we claim that it cannot be defined, even if it is said to dwell in the holy body of the Virgin, but rather that it fills the heavens as God, and the earth, and the things below, and is not absent from any of the whole. And there was also a human being after this.

The divine nature is not something that can be harmed or affected by its association with human nature. Just as the sun's light is not harmed by shining on the mire and marshes, the divine nature remains unharmed and unchanged. Those who think that they can share in the divine glory and define the unseemly as part of the best economy are mistaken. They do not accept the mystery of the divine nature, and are instead puffed up with pride and haughtiness.

Those who laugh at our beliefs think that the matter is foolish and that we are compared to lifeless objects. They do not understand that their own teachers, if they had grasped something to think or say, would have difficulty in keeping the faith and the saying 'He himself said', and then they would have opposed their own thoughts to the divine judgments, pouring them into their own heads with great difficulty. They do not honor these things with the divine nature, but rather think that someone has thoroughly investigated the matter. For they ask how the undefiled mind, which is free from quantity and definition, can be enclosed in a human body.

It is said that it is a small thing for the God who is above all to become like us. However, you accuse Him because, being philanthropic and good by nature, He has taken more care for us than is fitting. This is acknowledged to be a small thing for Him, which is called kenosis. Nevertheless, the word of His gentleness towards us will be shown to be consistent with Scripture. What is truly worthy of wonder is that He has taken on the causes of our salvation. One might ask how He has done this without being impious. Tell me, then, whether you think it would have been better for Him to leave us bound by our sins, or rather to save us and show us care. How can one doubt that it is fitting for the good God to distribute goods to those who have come from Him?

We will allow doctors to deal with the treatment of passions, but we will rebuke God for not being ignorant of the way of our care. For it would be absurd to think that God, who is above all, would not know the way of our care, and would not take care of us in a way that is fitting for Him.
